c.v: A motorcycle crash in Sterling Heights is governed by a rule many riders learn only after they are hurt: under Michigan no-fault, a motorcycle is not a “motor vehicle.” That definition decides who pays your medical bills, how much they pay, whether you have a no-fault claim at all, and how the insurer will argue the helmet question. Sterling Heights adds its own risks: Van Dyke, where a car turns left across the rider’s lane at every signal; the 18½ Mile roundabout, first in Michigan for crashes in 2025, where Van Dyke becomes the M-53 freeway; Hall Road’s retail traffic in summer riding season; concrete joints, patches, and potholes on the mile roads; and three road agencies, each with its own notice clock when the road itself caused the crash.

sections.heading: Where Sterling Heights motorcycle crashes happen

c.v: The left turn on Van Dyke, Hall Road, and the mile roads.

A driver turning left across oncoming traffic, misjudging the speed of a motorcycle or not seeing it at all, is the recurring account in rider cases. Under Michigan law a driver must yield to oncoming traffic before turning left (MCL 257.650). The 15, 16, and 17 Mile intersections on Van Dyke, the Hall Road signals, and the plant driveways produce the same crash at different speeds.
The M-53 merge.

At 18½ Mile, Van Dyke becomes a freeway. Drivers accelerating to merge and changing lanes to reach Hall Road or the M-59 interchange a mile north often fail to check for a motorcycle in the next lane.
Plant traffic.
Tractor-trailers turning wide into the plant gates on Van Dyke and Mound, and trucks stopped in travel lanes, are hazards a car can absorb and a motorcycle cannot. See our
Sterling Heights truck accident page
Hall Road (M-59).
Retail traffic pulling in and out of shopping centers and restaurants across the north of the city, with riders sharing the road on summer evenings with drivers leaving bars.
The road itself.

A single-vehicle crash caused by a pothole, a broken concrete joint, a pavement drop-off, or gravel is a claim against the agency with jurisdiction under the highway exception to governmental immunity (MCL 691.1402). In Sterling Heights that means three possible defendants:

items.v: MDOT for Van Dyke, Hall Road, and the M-53 freeway: written notice filed with the Court of Claims within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).

c.v: The Macomb County Department of Roads

items.v: for the mile roads, Mound, Schoenherr, Ryan, Dequindre, and Hayes: written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).

c.v: The City of Sterling Heights

items.v: for local streets: written notice within 120 days (MCL 691.1404).

c.v: A defect that was readily apparent to an ordinary observer for 30 days or more is conclusively presumed known to the agency (MCL 691.1403). Notice to the wrong agency is not notice.
Bars and restaurants.

31 percent of Michigan’s 2024 rider deaths involved alcohol. A bar that over-served the driver who hit a rider can be liable under the dram shop act: written notice within 120 days after you hire a lawyer, and suit within two years (MCL 436.1801(3)). See our
drunk driving accident page

sections.heading: Who pays a Sterling Heights rider’s medical bills

c.v: If a car or truck was involved, you have no-fault benefits, but not from your motorcycle insurer.
Under MCL 500.3114(5), your Personal Injury Protection benefits come, in order, from:

items.v: the insurer of the owner or registrant of the motor vehicle involved;
the insurer of that vehicle’s operator;
the motor vehicle insurer of the motorcycle’s operator;
the motor vehicle insurer of the motorcycle’s owner or registrant.

c.v: “Involved” does not require contact; a car that cut you off is involved even if it never touched you. If no insurer in that chain exists, the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan pays (MCL 500.3172), with its $250,000 medical cap, unless you owned the motorcycle and it was uninsured (MCL 500.3113(b)).

The benefits are the ones a driver would get under MCL 500.3107: medical expenses up to the PIP limit on the policy that pays, 85 percent of lost wages for up to three years up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each October, $20 a day in replacement services, attendant care, and mileage. Written notice is due within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). See our
no-fault insurance claim page

The first medical limit is set by a policy you did not choose. Since the 2019 reform, the PIP medical level on the policy first in priority pays first; if the driver who hit you chose $250,000, that policy pays up to $250,000, and a lower-priority policy with more coverage, such as your own car policy, may then pay the rest.
If no car or truck was involved, no-fault does not apply.

A single-vehicle crash on a pothole, a broken joint, or gravel produces no PIP claim. Your bills go to your health insurance and any medical coverage you bought on the motorcycle policy, and your injury claim is against whoever caused the hazard. Some summaries say motorcycles are simply “not included” in no-fault; that is true of the definition, but a rider hit by a car usually has a full PIP claim.
Your motorcycle.
Covered by your own collision coverage, or by the mini tort claim against the at-fault driver for up to $3,000 (MCL 500.3135(3)(e)), filed in the 41A District Court if the insurer will not pay it.

sections.heading: Your claim against the driver who hit you

c.v: For pain and suffering and economic losses beyond no-fault, you sue the at-fault driver if your injury is a serious impairment of body function, permanent serious disfigurement, or death (MCL 500.3135). Motorcycle injuries clear that threshold more often than car injuries: fractures, road rash requiring grafts, torn ligaments,
brain injuries
, and
spinal cord injuries
. You also recover excess economic damages above the PIP limit that applied to you (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)). You have three years to sue (MCL 600.5805(2)); a fatal crash is brought by the estate (see our
Sterling Heights wrongful death page
What the claim is worth depends on the other driver’s policy.
Many Sterling Heights drivers carry the $50,000 minimum, and some carry nothing. The recovery then turns on your own
uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage
, which must be on the motorcycle policy; many car policies exclude the insured while riding an owned motorcycle. See our
uninsured motorist page
Comparative fault is the fight.

Above 50 percent at fault you recover no noneconomic damages; below that your award is reduced by your share (MCL 500.3135(2)(b), 600.2959). Insurers argue speed, lane position, lane splitting (illegal in Michigan), and “came out of nowhere.” The police report, witnesses, the other driver’s phone records, business and plant cameras along Van Dyke and Mound, and the rider’s own camera answer it.

Since 2012, Michigan has let riders 21 and older ride without a helmet if they carry at least $20,000 in first-party medical coverage and have either held a motorcycle endorsement for two years or passed an approved safety course (MCL 257.658). If you met those conditions, riding helmetless was legal, so it was not a traffic violation. In a head-injury case the insurer will argue a helmet would have reduced the injury, which is a damages argument for the jury, not a bar; in a leg or shoulder case it is irrelevant.

faqs.question: A car turned left in front of me on Van Dyke and I went down. Do I have a claim?

answer.v: Yes. A driver turning left must yield to oncoming traffic, and the car is “involved” under no-fault whether or not it touched you, so its owner’s insurer is first in line for your medical bills. Get the plate and witnesses before the car is gone.

faqs.question: I hit a pothole on 17 Mile. Who do I notify?

answer.v: The mile roads in Sterling Heights are generally the Macomb County Department of Roads’: written notice within 120 days stating the exact location, the defect, the injury, and the witnesses. A defect on Van Dyke or Hall Road is MDOT’s, with written notice filed in the Court of Claims within 120 days.

A motorcycle is not a “motor vehicle” under the no-fault act, so a rider who crashes alone has no PIP claim. A rider hit by a car or truck does: from that vehicle’s insurer first, under the priority rule.

faqs.question: I wasn’t wearing a helmet. Can I still recover?

answer.v: Yes, if you were 21 or older with the required $20,000 medical coverage and either two years of endorsement or a safety course. The insurer can argue a helmet would have reduced a head injury, which goes to damages, not to whether you have a claim.

One year to notify the responsible no-fault insurer, three years to sue the at-fault driver, two years to sue a bar, 120 days for a notice to the City or the Department of Roads, and 120 days to file notice of a road-defect claim against the State.
